blocks.heading: The only hard problem
text: Caleb pays Nora 0.05 BTC. Ninety seconds later he signs a second transaction spending the same coin back to himself.
Both are valid. That sentence is the reason this chapter exists.

blocks.heading: First, what is _not_ hard
text: Spending a coin twice in sequence is trivial to catch. The second transaction names an input that is already gone, and every node rejects it without asking anyone.
Digital money is not hard to protect from copying. Hashes and signatures already did that.

blocks.heading: The hard case
text: Two transactions spending the same coin, where nobody has seen both.

blocks.alt: One coin feeding two conflicting transactions, one seen first in Lisbon and one in Toronto, both marked as verifying
blocks.caption: Caleb sends one to a peer in Lisbon and one to a peer in Toronto. Neither is malformed.

blocks.heading: Nora's node is not confused
text: It saw the payment, it verified, it is correct. A node in Toronto saw the other one, verified it, and is also correct.
There is no disagreement about the mathematics. The disagreement is about **which came first**, and neither of them can settle that.

blocks.heading: There is no clock to appeal to
text: Timestamps are written by whoever made the message. The 2-hour window from lesson 11 is a sanity check, not a clock.
Across a network with real latency, "first" is not a property of the world. It is a property of where you were standing.

blocks.question: Why not just have the nodes vote, and take the transaction the majority saw first?
answer: Because identities are free. Nothing stops Caleb running ten thousand nodes on rented machines, all voting for his version.
Any scheme where votes cost nothing is decided by whoever can be bothered to create the most participants. A vote has to be attached to something scarce, or it means nothing.

blocks.heading: The problem has a name and a literature
text: Lamport, Shostak and Pease posed it in 1982 as the Byzantine Generals Problem: reaching agreement when some participants send different messages to different peers.
Caleb is not a faulty node. He is a lying one, and lying deliberately in two directions at once.

blocks.heading: And a proof that it cannot be done

blocks.title: FLP, 1985
text: Fischer, Lynch and Paterson proved that in an asynchronous network, no deterministic protocol guarantees agreement if even one process may fail.
Not "nobody has found one". There is not one. Any design claiming to decide, definitively, at a moment in time, is wrong about something.

blocks.question: Bitcoin is an asynchronous network full of failing and lying nodes. So how does it get around a theorem?
answer: It does not. It changes the goal.

Bitcoin never decides anything at an instant. It makes disagreement progressively more expensive to sustain, so the probability of a reversal falls towards zero without ever reaching it. Agreement becomes something you get _more of_ by waiting.

blocks.heading: So this is the shape of what is needed
text: A tiebreak that cannot be forged, cannot be created for free, and that everyone arrives at independently without talking to each other.
Signatures cannot do it - Caleb signed both. Hashes cannot do it - both hash fine. Voting cannot do it - identities are free.
What is left is to make ordering cost something real.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: The problem was never forgery. It was that "first" has no meaning in a network, until somebody pays to give it one.
Nora is standing in her workshop with a synthesiser in a crate, deciding whether to ship it. Next: what the machines competing to answer her are actually doing.
